ku_excerpts.KU-0001: The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949
ku_excerpts.KU-0002: the Fundamental Rights in Part III entered into force on 26 January 1950
ku_excerpts.KU-0003: Fundamental Rights are contained in Articles 12 to 35 of the Constitution
ku_excerpts.KU-0004: They are justiciable, which means a citizen can move the Supreme Court under Article 32 or a High Court under Article 226 when a right is violated
ku_excerpts.KU-0005: The term 'State' under Article 12 includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and legislature of each State, all local authorities, and all other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India
ku_excerpts.KU-0006: 'Law' under Article 13 includes any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of India
ku_excerpts.KU-0007: all laws in force before 26 January 1950 that are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void to the extent of the inconsistency
ku_excerpts.KU-0008: bars the State from making any law that takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III
ku_excerpts.KU-0009: The First Amendment of 1951 added clause (4) to Article 13 protection for land-reform laws and inserted Articles 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule
ku_excerpts.KU-0010: The Forty-second Amendment of 1976 attempted to shield all Directive Principles from Articles 14 and 19
ku_excerpts.KU-0011: the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978 rolled back the worst excesses of the Emergency and deleted the right to property as a Fundamental Right
ku_excerpts.KU-0012: 1951: the First Amendment adds Articles 31A, 31B and Article 15(4)
ku_excerpts.KU-0013: 1976: the Forty-second Amendment inserts Articles 14A-related changes and the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity into the Preamble
ku_excerpts.KU-0014: 1992: the Supreme Court decides Indra Sawhney and caps reservations at 50 percent
ku_excerpts.KU-0015: 2002: the Eighty-sixth Amendment inserts Article 21A on free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years
ku_excerpts.KU-0016: 2009: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act is passed to enforce Article 21A
ku_excerpts.KU-0017: 2015: the Supreme Court strikes down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
ku_excerpts.KU-0018: 2017: the nine-judge bench in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India declares privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21
ku_excerpts.KU-0019: 2019: the One Hundred and Third Amendment inserts Articles 15(6) and 16(6) providing up to 10 percent reservation for Economically Weaker Sections
ku_excerpts.KU-0020: Article 14 | Equality before law and equal protection | No person denied equality; reasonable classification allowed
ku_excerpts.KU-0021: Article 15 | No discrimination on listed grounds | Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; exceptions in clauses (3) to (6)
ku_excerpts.KU-0022: Article 16 | Equality in public employment | Equal opportunity; residence and reservation exceptions
ku_excerpts.KU-0023: Article 19 | Six freedoms | Speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession
ku_excerpts.KU-0024: Article 21 | Life and personal liberty | No deprivation except by procedure established by law
ku_excerpts.KU-0025: Article 32 | Right to Constitutional Remedies | Move the Supreme Court; called the heart and soul of the Constitution
ku_excerpts.KU-0026: Article 12 | Definition of State | Government, Parliament, legislatures, local and other authorities
ku_excerpts.KU-0027: Article 13 | Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights | Pre-1950 inconsistent laws void; State cannot abridge Part III
ku_excerpts.KU-0028: Article 17 | Abolition of untouchability | Practice forbidden; offence punishable by law
ku_excerpts.KU-0029: Article 18 | Abolition of titles | No State titles except military and academic distinctions
ku_excerpts.KU-0030: Article 20 | Protection in convictions | No ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination
ku_excerpts.KU-0031: Article 21A | Free and compulsory education | Children aged 6 to 14 years; inserted in 2002
ku_excerpts.KU-0032: Article 22 | Protection against arrest and detention | Informed of grounds; preventive detention limits
ku_excerpts.KU-0033: Article 23 | No trafficking or forced labour | Begar and bonded labour prohibited
ku_excerpts.KU-0034: Article 24 | No child labour in hazardous work | Children below 14 years barred from factories and mines
ku_excerpts.KU-0035: Articles 25 to 28 | Freedom of religion | Conscience, practice, propagation, management, no religious taxes
ku_excerpts.KU-0036: Articles 29 to 30 | Cultural and educational rights | Minority language, script, culture; minority institutions
ku_excerpts.KU-0037: Definition: 'Equality before the law' means the absence of any special privilege for any person, while 'equal protection of the laws' means equals must be treated equally and a reasonable classification of persons is permitted
ku_excerpts.KU-0038: Distinction: equality before the law is a negative concept that denies special privilege, whereas equal protection of the laws is a positive concept that permits reasonable classification of equals and unequals
ku_excerpts.KU-0039: Article 14 covers all persons, citizens and non-citizens alike
ku_excerpts.KU-0040: rests on an intelligible differentia and the differentia has a rational relation to the object of the law
ku_excerpts.KU-0041: Distinction: Article 15 prohibits discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, whereas Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity more broadly in matters of public employment
ku_excerpts.KU-0042: Article 15 applies to both the State and, in some clauses, private individuals running public places such as shops, wells, roads and places of public resort
ku_excerpts.KU-0043: Article 16 applies to employment under the State
ku_excerpts.KU-0044: Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children, Article 15(4) added in 1951 permits special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes
ku_excerpts.KU-0045: Articles 15(5) and 15(6) extend reservations to private educational institutions and to Economically Weaker Sections respectively
ku_excerpts.KU-0046: Article 16(4) permits reservation in favour of backward classes, Article 16(4A) permits reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and Article 16(6) inserted in 2019 permits up to 10 percent reservation for Economically Weaker Sections
ku_excerpts.KU-0047: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens only, a point examiners repeat every year
ku_excerpts.KU-0048: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a)
ku_excerpts.KU-0049: Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms under Article 19(1)(b)
ku_excerpts.KU-0050: Freedom to form associations or unions under Article 19(1)(c)
ku_excerpts.KU-0051: Freedom to move freely throughout India under Article 19(1)(d)
ku_excerpts.KU-0052: Freedom to reside and settle in any part of India under Article 19(1)(e)
ku_excerpts.KU-0053: Freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business under Article 19(1)(g)
ku_excerpts.KU-0054: Note that the original clause (f) on property was removed by the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978
ku_excerpts.KU-0055: Each freedom is subject to reasonable restrictions in clauses (2) to (6), including the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence
ku_excerpts.KU-0056: In 2015 the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act because vague limits on online speech were not reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)
ku_excerpts.KU-0057: Distinction: Article 19 protects the freedoms of citizens only, whereas Article 21 protects the life and liberty of all persons including non-citizens
ku_excerpts.KU-0058: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law
ku_excerpts.KU-0059: in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India in 1978 the Supreme Court held that the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable and not arbitrary or oppressive
ku_excerpts.KU-0060: whereas 'due process of law' additionally demands that the law itself be fair and reasonable, and after Maneka Gandhi in 1978 the Court reads Article 21 as including due-process values
ku_excerpts.KU-0061: the Court has read many implied rights into Article 21, including the right to live with dignity, livelihood, shelter, health, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid, and, in 2017, privacy in the Puttaswamy judgment
ku_excerpts.KU-0062: Article 21A on education for children aged 6 to 14 years was inserted by the Eighty-sixth Amendment in 2002 and enforced through the 2009 education Act
ku_excerpts.KU-0063: Definition: 'Preventive detention' means detention of a person without trial on the apprehension that the person may commit a future offence, whereas punitive detention follows conviction for an offence already committed
ku_excerpts.KU-0064: Article 32 gives every citizen the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights
ku_excerpts.KU-0065: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution
ku_excerpts.KU-0066: The Supreme Court has held that Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right, so Parliament cannot suspend it by an ordinary law
ku_excerpts.KU-0067: Habeas corpus: to produce a detained person before the court
ku_excerpts.KU-0068: Mandamus: to command a public authority to perform a legal duty
ku_excerpts.KU-0069: Prohibition: to restrain a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction
ku_excerpts.KU-0070: Certiorari: to quash the order of a lower court or tribunal
ku_excerpts.KU-0071: Quo warranto: to question the authority by which a person holds a public office
ku_excerpts.KU-0072: Definition: A 'writ' is a written order issued by a constitutional court commanding a person or authority to do, or to refrain from doing, a specified act
ku_excerpts.KU-0073: Distinction: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and the Supreme Court must grant a remedy when a Fundamental Right is violated, whereas Article 226 is wider in scope but discretionary, covering Fundamental Rights and other legal rights before a High Court
ku_excerpts.KU-0074: the majority in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla in 1976 held that Article 21 could be suspended
ku_excerpts.KU-0075: the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978 then provided that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an Emergency
ku_excerpts.KU-0076: The state covers about 78,438 square kilometres
ku_excerpts.KU-0077: the Brahmaputra valley is roughly 720 kilometres long from east to west and 80 to 100 kilometres wide
ku_excerpts.KU-0078: The Brahmaputra is a braided river across most of Assam, shifting channels, building sandbars called chars, and flooding heavily every monsoon
ku_excerpts.KU-0079: Definition: A 'braided river' is a wide, shallow river that splits into many interlacing channels around temporary sandbars and islands
ku_excerpts.KU-0080: Definition: 'Alluvium' is fertile silt, sand and clay deposited by rivers, and the Brahmaputra valley floor is almost entirely recent alluvium

ku_excerpts.KU-0106: Assam has three broad soil zones: recent alluvial soils of the flood plains, old alluvial soils of the higher terraces, and laterite and red soils on the Karbi and Dima Hasao hills with patches of forest soil
ku_excerpts.KU-0107: Distinction: khadar soils are newer, finer, low-lying alluvium renewed by almost every flood, whereas bhangar soils are older, coarser, higher-lying alluvium above the normal flood limit
ku_excerpts.KU-0108: The climate is humid subtropical with a strong monsoon
ku_excerpts.KU-0109: Average annual rainfall for the state is about 2,300 millimetres
ku_excerpts.KU-0110: with Cherrapunji-Mawsynram just across the border in Meghalaya receiving over 11,000 millimetres in extreme years
ku_excerpts.KU-0111: Summer temperatures range from 30 to 35 degrees Celsius in the valley, winter minimums fall to 6 to 10 degrees Celsius, and relative humidity stays between 70 and 85 percent for much of the year
ku_excerpts.KU-0112: Roughly 75 percent of annual rain falls between June and September
ku_excerpts.KU-0113: the devastating floods of 2022 affected all 35 districts and over 5.8 million people
ku_excerpts.KU-0114: the 2011 census recorded Assam at about 31.2 million people with a density near 398 persons per square kilometre
